title: Normalized homology surjectivity descends through free abelian evaluation
statement: Let $X,Y$ be simplicial abelian groups and $f:X\to Y$ an additive simplicial morphism [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-object]. For a simplicial set $S$, let $F(S)_m=\mathbb Z[S_m]$, the free abelian group with basis vectors $[s]$ indexed by $s\in S_m$; every simplicial operator acts by $[s]\mapsto[S(\varphi)(s)]$. For a simplicial-set map $a:S\to T$ put $F(a)_m([s])=[a_m(s)]$. Write $UZ$ for the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial abelian group $Z$ [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set]. Let $\epsilon_Z:F(UZ)\to Z$ be evaluation, given degreewise by $\sum_j a_j[z_j]\mapsto\sum_j a_jz_j$. For a simplicial abelian group $Z$ [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-object], set $N(Z)_0=Z_0$ and $N(Z)_m=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\ker(d_i:Z_m\to Z_{m-1})$ for $m>0$, with differential $\partial_m=d_0$ for $m>0$ and $\partial_0=0$. Write $H_m(N(Z))=\ker\partial_m/\operatorname{im}\partial_{m+1}$; a simplicial morphism $a$ induces the chain map $N(a)$ by restriction in every degree. The evaluation maps are simplicial morphisms and satisfy $f\circ\epsilon_X=\epsilon_Y\circ F(Uf)$. For every $n\geq0$ and cycle $y\in N(Y)_n$, the element $\widetilde y=[y]-[0_n]\in F(UY)_n$ is a cycle of $N(F(UY))$ evaluating to $y$; here $0_m$ denotes the zero simplex in degree $m$. Consequently, for every fixed $n\geq0$, if $H_n(N(F(Uf)))$ is surjective then $H_n(N(f))$ is surjective.

proof.text: For every simplicial operator $\varphi$, the formula $[s]\mapsto[S(\varphi)(s)]$ respects identity and composition on each generator, hence on every finite integral sum. The same calculation shows that $F(a)$ commutes with the operators for a simplicial-set map $a$. For an abelian simplicial object $Z$, additivity gives $Z(\varphi)(\sum_j a_jz_j)=\sum_j a_jZ(\varphi)(z_j)$, which is exactly $Z(\varphi)\epsilon_Z=\epsilon_ZF(UZ)(\varphi)$. Thus evaluation is simplicial. On a generator $[x]$, both $f\epsilon_X$ and $\epsilon_YF(Uf)$ equal $f(x)$; additivity proves the displayed square on all elements.

proof.text: The normalization is a complex: for $z\in N(Z)_m$ and $m\geq2$, the simplicial identities give $d_i d_0z=d_0d_{i+1}z=0$ for $1\leq i\leq m-1$, and $d_0d_0z=d_0d_1z=0$. For $m=1$, the target is $N(Z)_0=Z_0$ and the next differential is zero. If $a$ is simplicial and additive, $d_i a_m(z)=a_{m-1}(d_i z)$ shows that $a$ preserves each normalized subgroup and commutes with its differential (also in degree zero). Consequently it takes cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries, so restriction defines the indicated maps on the quotient groups $H_n$. These observations apply in particular to the three maps of the evaluation square.

source.place: Tag 08P2, lemma-homotopy-equivalence, evaluation square and surjectivity paragraph (lines 5895–5932); with the explicitly stated d_0 normalization.

proof.text: Let $y\in N(Y)_n$ be a cycle. For $n>0$, normalization gives $d_i y=0$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ and the cycle condition gives $d_0y=0$. Since each face is additive, $d_i0_n=0_{n-1}$; thus every face of $\widetilde y=[y]-[0_n]$ is $[0_{n-1}]-[0_{n-1}]=0$. This proves both normalization and the cycle condition for $\widetilde y$. For $n=0$, normalization imposes no condition and the differential is zero, so the same conclusion holds without mentioning a degree $-1$ face. In every degree, $\epsilon_Y(\widetilde y)=y-0_n=y$.

source.place: Tag 08P2, lemma-homotopy-equivalence, evaluation square and surjectivity paragraph (lines 5895–5932); with the explicitly stated d_0 normalization.

proof.text: Fix $n$ and assume $H_n(N(F(Uf)))$ is surjective. Represent any class of $H_n(N(Y))$ by a cycle $y$, and lift it to the cycle $\widetilde y$ of the preceding step. Surjectivity supplies a cycle $u\in N(F(UX))_n$ whose homology class maps to that of $\widetilde y$. By the definition of equality modulo boundaries there is $v\in N(F(UY))_{n+1}$ with $F(Uf)_n(u)-\widetilde y=\partial_{n+1}v$. Set $x=\epsilon_X(u)$; it is a normalized cycle by step 2. Evaluating the last equality and using the square of step 1 gives $f_n(x)-y=\partial_{n+1}\epsilon_Y(v)$, with $\epsilon_Y(v)\in N(Y)_{n+1}$. Hence the class of $x$ maps to the prescribed class of $y$. This works also for $n=0$, proving the required surjectivity.
